title: Organelles and compartmentalization
summary: Organelles are discrete subunits that divide eukaryotic cells into compartments, each suited to particular functions. HL looks at how mitochondria, chloroplasts, the nucleus, rough ER, Golgi apparatus and vesicles are adapted to their roles.

keyterms.definition: A discrete subunit of a cell adapted to perform a specific function; the cell wall, cytoskeleton and cytoplasm are not organelles.
Division of the cell into membrane-bound compartments, allowing high local concentrations of enzymes and substrates and separating incompatible processes.
Double membrane that separates the nucleus from the cytoplasm, so transcription and translation occur in different compartments.
Processing of mRNA in the nucleus, e.g. removal of introns, before it reaches ribosomes; impossible in prokaryotes, where translation can start immediately.
Membrane-bound vesicle containing hydrolytic enzymes, kept separate from the cytoplasm so they do not digest the cell's own components.
Vacuole formed when a cell engulfs material by endocytosis; lysosomes fuse with it to digest the contents.
Separating organelles from a cell homogenate by spinning at increasing speeds, so they sediment according to size and density.
Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane giving a large surface area for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.
Small space between the inner and outer mitochondrial membranes, in which a proton gradient builds up quickly.
Fluid inside the inner mitochondrial membrane containing enzymes of the link reaction and Krebs cycle.
Flattened membrane sac in a chloroplast holding photosynthetic pigments, photosystems and ATP synthase; stacks are called grana.
Fluid of the chloroplast surrounding the thylakoids, containing enzymes of the Calvin cycle.
Protein-lined opening in the nuclear envelope allowing controlled exchange, e.g. mRNA out and proteins in.
Ribosomes on rough ER make proteins for secretion, lysosomes or membranes; free ribosomes make proteins for use in the cytosol.
Stack of flattened membrane sacs (cisternae) that modifies, sorts and packages proteins from the rough ER into vesicles.
Protein that coats membranes and helps them bud off to form vesicles, e.g. in endocytosis.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an organelle?
options: Cytoskeleton
Cell wall
Mitochondrion
Cytoplasm
questions.explanation: A mitochondrion is a discrete subunit with a specific function. The cell wall is outside the plasma membrane, the cytoskeleton is a network spread through the cell, and the cytoplasm is everything inside the membrane except the nucleus.

questions.statement: The cell wall of a plant cell is classified as an organelle.
questions.explanation: The cell wall is an extracellular structure outside the plasma membrane, not a discrete subunit within the cell, so it is not an organelle.

questions.text: A discrete subunit of a cell that is adapted to perform a specific function is called an ___.
questions.explanation: Organelles divide the work of the cell; tissues and organs are levels of organization made of many cells.

questions.prompt: Match each organelle to its function.
questions.explanation: Each organelle has a structure suited to one main function, which is the basis of the division of labour within the cell.

questions.prompt: Why did the development of ultracentrifugation advance our understanding of organelles?
options: It allowed organelles to be seen in colour for the first time
It separated organelles by size and density so the function of each could be studied in isolation
It showed that organelles move around the cell
It increased the resolution of light microscopes
questions.explanation: Cell fractionation isolates fractions rich in one organelle type, so scientists could test which reactions each fraction carries out. Progress in science often follows new techniques like this.

questions.statement: Ribosomes are found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
questions.explanation: All cells make proteins, so all have ribosomes; prokaryotic ribosomes (70S) are smaller than those in the eukaryotic cytoplasm (80S).

questions.prompt: Put the steps of cell fractionation in order.
items: Tissue is homogenized in cold, isotonic buffer
Low-speed spin: nuclei form a pellet
Higher-speed spin of the supernatant: mitochondria form a pellet
Highest-speed spin: ribosomes form a pellet
questions.explanation: Larger, denser organelles sediment at lower speeds, so the supernatant is re-spun faster each time to collect progressively smaller organelles.

questions.prompt: In cell fractionation, why is the homogenate kept in an isotonic solution?
options: To speed up enzyme activity
To make organelles denser so they sediment faster
To dissolve the cell walls
To prevent organelles gaining or losing water by osmosis and being damaged
questions.explanation: An isotonic solution has the same solute concentration as the organelles, so there is no net osmosis and they do not burst or shrink. Keeping it cold reduces enzyme activity that could damage them.

questions.text: The ___ is not an organelle but a network of protein filaments that maintains cell shape and moves organelles.
questions.explanation: The cytoskeleton runs throughout the cytoplasm rather than being a discrete subunit, so it is not counted as an organelle.

questions.prompt: Which organelle is found in many plant cells but never in animal cells?
options: Chloroplast
Mitochondrion
Ribosome
Golgi apparatus
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis and occur in plants and algae. Mitochondria, ribosomes and the Golgi apparatus are found in both plant and animal cells.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of separating the nucleus from the cytoplasm?
options: It protects DNA from all mutations
It allows translation to begin while transcription is still happening
It allows mRNA to be modified before translation begins
It keeps ribosomes close to the chromosomes
questions.explanation: Because ribosomes are outside the nucleus, mRNA can be processed (e.g. introns removed) before any of it is translated, so only mature mRNA is used.

questions.statement: In prokaryotes, ribosomes can begin translating an mRNA while it is still being transcribed.
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes have no nuclear membrane, so transcription and translation occur in the same compartment and can be coupled; mRNA cannot first be modified.

questions.text: In eukaryotes, mRNA is ___ in the nucleus before it is exported to ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
questions.explanation: Post-transcriptional modification happens inside the nucleus; translation only takes place once mRNA has reached the cytoplasm.

questions.prompt: Why is it an advantage that hydrolytic enzymes are kept inside lysosomes?
options: They work faster when diluted in the cytoplasm
They would otherwise digest the cell's own molecules and organelles
Lysosomes are the only place where ATP is available
It allows the enzymes to be secreted constantly
questions.explanation: Compartmentalization separates incompatible processes: enzymes that digest biological molecules must be isolated from the rest of the cell.

questions.prompt: Match each advantage of compartmentalization to an example.

pairs.right: Krebs cycle enzymes in the mitochondrial matrix
Nuclear envelope separating transcription and translation
Lysosomes fusing with a phagocytic vacuole

questions.explanation: Membranes let each compartment keep its own contents and conditions, so reactions run efficiently and do not interfere with one another.

questions.statement: Phagocytic vacuoles let white blood cells digest ingested pathogens without hydrolytic enzymes damaging the cytoplasm.
questions.explanation: Digestion happens inside the membrane-bound vacuole after lysosomes fuse with it, so the enzymes never reach the cytoplasm.

questions.text: When a phagocyte engulfs a bacterium, a ___ forms around it, and lysosomes then fuse with it.
questions.explanation: Engulfing by endocytosis encloses the bacterium in a membrane-bound phagocytic vacuole, which becomes a digestion compartment.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of pathogen digestion by a phagocyte in order.
questions.explanation: The pathogen is enclosed first, then the lysosomes deliver their enzymes into the vacuole so digestion is contained.

questions.prompt: How does compartmentalization make metabolic pathways more efficient?
options: It removes the need for enzymes
It makes every compartment the same pH
It allows all reactions to happen in one place at once
Enzymes and metabolites can be concentrated in a small volume, so reactions happen faster
questions.explanation: Higher concentrations of enzymes and substrates within a compartment increase the rate of collisions, so pathways proceed more quickly.

questions.prompt: Which statement about prokaryotic cells is correct?
options: They lack a nucleus, so transcription and translation occur in the same compartment
They modify mRNA in the nucleoid before translation
They contain lysosomes for digestion of pathogens
Their DNA is separated from ribosomes by a double membrane
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound nucleus or other membrane-bound organelles, so their DNA and ribosomes share the cytoplasm.

questions.prompt: How does the small volume of the mitochondrial intermembrane space help ATP production?
options: It stores ATP until it is needed
A steep proton gradient builds up quickly from relatively few protons pumped
It contains the enzymes of the Krebs cycle
It allows oxygen to diffuse in faster
questions.explanation: Protons pumped by the electron transport chain accumulate in the small space, rapidly creating the concentration gradient that drives ATP synthase.

questions.text: The inner mitochondrial membrane is folded into ___, increasing the surface area for electron transport chains and ATP synthase.
questions.explanation: More inner membrane means more electron transport chains and ATP synthase molecules, so more ATP can be made.

questions.prompt: Match each region to what it contains.

pairs.right: Enzymes of the link reaction and Krebs cycle
Electron transport chains and ATP synthase

questions.explanation: Both organelles separate membrane-based reactions (electron transport, ATP synthesis) from fluid compartments containing the enzymes of cyclic pathways.

questions.statement: The small volume inside the thylakoids allows a proton gradient to build up quickly.
questions.explanation: Protons are pumped into the thylakoid space during the light-dependent reactions; its small volume means the concentration rises quickly, driving ATP synthase.

questions.prompt: Why are thylakoids arranged in large numbers and stacked into grana?
options: To store starch produced by photosynthesis
To increase the volume of the stroma
To protect the chloroplast DNA
To provide a large membrane surface area for pigments and photosystems to absorb light
questions.explanation: Light absorption and the light-dependent reactions take place on thylakoid membranes, so a large membrane area increases the rate of photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: What is the function of nuclear pores?
options: They control exchange between nucleus and cytoplasm, e.g. mRNA out and proteins in, while DNA stays inside
They let ribosomes enter the nucleus to translate mRNA
They allow chromosomes to leave the nucleus during interphase
They pump protons into the nucleus
questions.explanation: The double nuclear membrane keeps DNA protected, while pores allow regulated traffic such as mRNA export and import of proteins like DNA polymerase.

questions.statement: During mitosis the nuclear envelope breaks into vesicles, which later fuse to reform a nucleus around each set of chromosomes.
questions.explanation: Breaking the envelope into vesicles frees the chromosomes for the spindle; the vesicles are reused to rebuild the nuclear envelopes in telophase.

questions.text: The outer membrane of the nuclear envelope is continuous with the ___.
questions.explanation: The outer nuclear membrane joins the rough ER and can also carry ribosomes, linking the nucleus to the protein-processing pathway.

questions.prompt: Which proteins are made by free ribosomes rather than ribosomes attached to rough ER?
options: Digestive enzymes secreted by pancreatic cells
Enzymes destined for lysosomes
Proteins for use within the cytosol, such as glycolysis enzymes
Hormones such as insulin
questions.explanation: Free ribosomes release proteins into the cytosol for use there. Proteins for secretion, lysosomes or membranes are made on rough ER and enter its lumen.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in the production and secretion of a protein in order.
items: Polypeptide is made by ribosomes on rough ER
Polypeptide enters the RER lumen and is folded
It is carried in a vesicle to the Golgi apparatus
It is modified and packaged in the Golgi apparatus
A vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane by exocytosis
questions.explanation: Secreted proteins travel from rough ER to Golgi to plasma membrane inside vesicles, so they never enter the cytosol.

questions.prompt: What is the role of clathrin?
options: It pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane
It digests material inside lysosomes
It forms pores in the nuclear envelope
It coats patches of membrane and helps them bud off as vesicles
questions.explanation: Clathrin forms a cage-like coat on the cytoplasmic side of a membrane, bending it into a vesicle, for example during endocytosis.

questions.statement: The Golgi apparatus receives vesicles from the rough ER on one face and releases vesicles of processed proteins from the opposite face.
questions.explanation: Vesicles from the ER fuse at the cis face; proteins are modified as they pass through the cisternae and leave in vesicles budding from the trans face.
